What are the relevant questions?
 Statistical models address specific questions
 Different growth analysis techniques answer (or fail to answer)
 different, but often related, questions
 It is critical to understanding these different questions.
 Answers to different questions often lead to different uses and
 outcomes.

 Questions form the vocabulary of later discussions
 Starting with the right questions simplifies both the development
 of appropriate analyses and motivating the proper use of the
 results.
 Clearly articulating the questions to be answered (which often
 differ by stakeholder group) sets the stage for subsequent
 conversations that will take place.

Why Growth in Accountability?

 Fundamental Premise
 “Good” schools bring about student growth in excess of that found at
 “bad” schools.

 The inherent believability of this premise is at the heart of current
 enthusiasm to incorporate growth models into state accountability
 systems.
 Note that current NCLB accountability invokes the same premise
 with achievement substituted for growth.
 In light of this premise, “good schools” are commonly referred to as
 highly effective schools.
 However, it is critical to understand the distinction between growth
 and effectiveness.

Value-added Models/Inferences
 Who/What is responsible for student growth?
 Currently, the most common analyses of student growth attempt to
 determine the amount of student progress/growth that can be
 attributed to the school or teacher.
 Called value-added analyses, these techniques estimate the
 teacher/school contribution to student achievement.
 Value-added models quantify effectiveness—purporting to measure
 the impact on achievement that this school or teacher would have,
 on average, upon similar students assigned to them.
 The foremost example being the value-added models developed by
 Dr. William Sanders and used in many school districts nationwide to
 infer teacher or school effectiveness.
 These models and their effectiveness claims are controversial for a
 number of reasons [Braun, 2005, Rubin et al., 2004].
 Value-added models are better described as effectiveness models
 than as growth models.

Descriptive Growth Models

 Describing Growth versus Ascribing Responsibility
 Yen’s questions make no mention of effectiveness.
 The questions point toward a description of student growth.
 An important first step in the development of Colorado’s Growth
 Model was to separate the description of growth from the
 assignment of responsibility (i.e., accountability)
 Incorporation of growth into the accountability system followed from
 the viable description of growth.
 What follows is an introduction to student growth percentiles—a
 normative description of growth that forms the basis of Colorado’s
 Growth Model.

Describing Actual Student Growth

 Measuring student growth, even with a vertical scale, is not a simple
 task.
 Numerous states believe that placing their tests on a vertical scale
 will simplify the task of measuring student growth.
 Even with an interval (or ratio) scale, growth is not easy to interpret.
 Consider, for example, height.
 A child might grow 4 inches between ages 3 and 4.
 4 inches is a well understood quantity.
 However, the 4 inch increase becomes fully understandable only when
 placed in context of growth of other children between ages 3 and 4.
 In the following discussion student growth percentiles are introduced
 to provide a normative context for interpreting student growth.

Student Growth Percentiles
 Given a student’s prior scale scores and the associated conditional
 density, their current scale score corresponds to a percentile of that
 conditional distribution.
 This percentile is the student’s growth percentile.
 For example, a student growth percentile of 60 indicates the student’s
 latest scale score exceeded 60 percent of his/her counterparts with
 equal prior scores.
 Growth percentiles are closely related to estimating the probability of
 observing a student’s current achievement taking account of their
 past achievement:

 Pr(Current Achievement |Past Achievement ).
 As such, growth percentiles describe the rarity of a student’s current
 achievement conditional upon their prior achievement.

Student Growth Percentiles
 Student growth percentiles norm each student’s growth relative to
 their academic peers.
 The percentile scale on which the growth percentiles lie allows for
 easy comparison of all students.
 For example, consider a low achieving student demonstrating 90th
 percentile growth and a high achieving student demonstrating 10th
 percentile growth.
 The low achieving student grew at a rate exceeding 90 percent of similar
 students.
 The high achieving student grew at a rate exceeding just 10 percent of
 similar students.
 In this sense, the low achiever’s growth is more exemplary than the high
 achiever’s.
 However, judgment of whether the student’s growth was adequate
 requires external criteria.

Combining Actual and Aspirational Growth

 Using student growth percentiles it is simple to reconcile actual
 growth measures with aspirational growth targets.
 Each student receives a growth percentile derived from present
 performance conditioning upon past performance.
 Growth standard setting is conducted to determine what growth
 percentiles will be considered adequate and what growth percentiles
 will be considered inadequate.
 For example, consider a student just completing the 5th grade
 Their reading was at the partially proficient level.
 However, considering their 3rd and 4th grade achievement, they grew
 in the last year at the 95th percentile.
